- 'heading "Black Friday: capacity testing that prevented an incident" [level=2]'
- heading "The setup" [level=3]
- paragraph: Ahead of Black Friday, the platform needed proven — not assumed — confidence that it could handle peak load. Performance testing started with JMeter and later moved to k6, running load simulations against expected and above-expected traffic patterns.
- heading "What testing found" [level=3]
- paragraph: Sustained load surfaced a memory leak — not a crash, not an obvious error, but a slow degradation invisible in short manual checks and guaranteed to surface hours into real peak traffic. Flagged early enough for dev and DevOps to act with real runway, not a last-minute scramble.
- heading "The outcome" [level=3]
- text: Traffic mitigated before ✓ Yes Peak volume handled 3,000+ applications/day Capacity incidents 0 Now standard practice ✓ Yes
- heading "Automated k6 performance history" [level=3]
- text: "Last run: Sep 14, 2026, 8:42 AM Load ✓ gates passed Stress ✓ gates passed Soak ✓ gates passed"

- text: "[CASE STUDY] Maturity assessment"
- heading "QA Maturity Assessment & Automation Transformation" [level=2]
- heading "Context" [level=3]
- paragraph: I initiated and led a QA maturity assessment across 13 teams. The initiative was independently identified as a need within the organization before the recent AI-driven automation wave made quality transformation a mainstream expectation. I identified the organizational QA gap before it became an obvious industry trend.
- heading "Approach" [level=3]
- paragraph: I designed the assessment myself and structured it into distinct evaluation categories covering the QA process across the SDLC. The assessment was detailed enough to identify specific process gaps from a QA perspective that were not being identified by other roles. Within the organization, the assessment was described as “pure gold” because of its thoroughness and usefulness. It focused on QA processes, test strategy, automation, SDLC integration, quality practices, release processes, risk identification, and gaps between development and QA.
- heading "Impact" [level=3]
- text: Key takeaway Leadership demonstrated through initiative, not title.
- paragraph: At the time of the assessment, the vast majority of teams had no test automation in place. Roughly a year later, automation adoption had grown to close to half of the teams, representing a significant increase in automation adoption influenced directly by the findings and recommendations from the assessment.
- heading "Leadership / influence" [level=3]
- paragraph: "This transformation was driven without holding a formal leadership title. It reflected leading without authority: identifying a cross-team problem, creating the assessment, communicating the findings, securing management buy-in, influencing multiple teams, and driving measurable change through initiative and technical influence."
- paragraph: "This initiative reflected a broader pattern in how I approach my work: identifying gaps before they are asked of me, and taking ownership of improvements even outside my formal scope. It reinforced my focus on deepening automation and engineering skills to drive quality through technical impact."
